intro: Five of these fifteen stand in the Prinsentuin, which has been an open public walking park for more than two hundred years and is one of the first in the Netherlands. It was laid out between 1822 and 1824 on the old northern ramparts by Lucas Pieters Roodbaard, the Frisian garden architect who also designed the city cemetery a few streets north, where herons now nest in the crowns of his plane trees. The oldest, and the one to see first, is a copper beech by the Westerkerk that the register says will eventually have to come down.
meta_description: Fifteen remarkable trees in Leeuwarden: five in the two-hundred-year-old Prinsentuin, a heron colony in a Roodbaard cemetery, and a beech on borrowed time.
question_meta: Leeuwarden's oldest tree is a copper beech by the Westerkerk, banded 1750 to 1800, and the register expects it will have to be felled.
question_answer: The oldest tree in Leeuwarden is a copper beech standing by the Westerkerk on the Sint Anthonystraat, which the national register places in a planting band of 1750 to 1800, so between about 225 and 275 years old. It is also the one tree here with a warning attached. The register records that its rooting ground was compacted in the 1990s, that the tree took a blow from which it never recovered, and that although the ground has since been improved its condition has not come back, so it will in time have to be felled. It is standing now. If you want to see the oldest tree in Leeuwarden, this is an argument for going this year rather than in ten.
question_context: Ages here come from the Landelijk Register Monumentale Bomen, which records a planting decade rather than a year, so every age on this page is a band and none is narrowed to look precise. The register is the 2024 edition and is the single source for most of these trees, which is why they are flagged. It is a careful source: for several of these it records the tree's condition as well as its age, which is where the note about the Westerkerk beech comes from and why we have passed it on rather than quietly leaving it out. The Prinsentuin trees are dated indirectly, because the register reasons from the park's own history that the oldest trees in it must come from between 1830 and 1880 rather than from a record of any individual planting. Pins are as the register surveyed them; where one is marked approximate we know the park and not the trunk.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Leeuwarden?
faq.a: A copper beech by the Westerkerk, banded 1750 to 1800. The register notes that its growing ground was compacted in the 1990s and its condition never recovered, and that it will eventually have to be felled.

It has been a public walking park for over two hundred years, which makes it one of the earliest in the Netherlands. The present layout was made between 1822 and 1824 in the existing garden on the former northern fortifications, by the Frisian garden architect Lucas Pieters Roodbaard, in the romantic style. The rampart and canal system it belongs to has been a national monument since 1967.

faq.q: Is there really a heron colony in the old cemetery?
faq.a: Yes. The Oude Stadsbegraafplaats on the Jelsummerstraat was laid out in 1833 to a Roodbaard design, is no longer in use and is a national monument. Grey herons nest in the crowns of its old trees and many of the trunks are grown over with ivy.

Yes. The Prinsentuin is an open public park, the old cemetery is open ground and no longer in use, and the Westerkerk beech stands on the street. The horse chestnut at Poptaslot, out at Marssum, stands in a garden that is free but keeps weekday hours, April to September, and is closed on Sundays.

trees.name: The Horse Chestnut of the Prinsentuin
trees.age_estimate: roughly 195 to 205 years, from the register's planting band of 1820 to 1830

location.address: Prinsentuin, Groeneweg 1, beside the Historisch Centrum

trees.story:
This tree is almost exactly as old as the idea of a public park in this country.

Between 1822 and 1824 the city had a new garden laid out on the northern fortifications, in the existing grounds, by Lucas Pieters Roodbaard, the Frisian garden architect who spent his career converting Dutch formality into the romantic English manner: curved paths, water, planned views, no straight lines. It has been open to the public ever since, which makes the Prinsentuin one of the first public walking parks in the Netherlands and this chestnut one of the original plantings.

Two hundred years of people walking under a tree is not neutral. Horse chestnuts suffer badly from compacted ground and this one has had two centuries of feet. It is also the species now under attack across Europe from the leaf miner moth, which browns the foliage from July onward and makes a mature chestnut look half dead by August without actually killing it.

So come in May, when it is at its unarguable best: white candles held upright all over the crown, in a park laid out by a man who would have chosen it for exactly that.

It stands beside the Historisch Centrum, on the Groeneweg side.
verified_sources: https://www.monumentalebomen.nl/
trees.transport: About 1 km north of Leeuwarden station, on foot.
trees.how_to_recognise: The big chestnut on the Groeneweg side of the park, next to the Historisch Centrum. In May it is covered in upright white flower spikes.

best_time.label: May, when the white candles are up across the whole crown

trees.name: The Copper Beech of the Westerkerk
trees.age_estimate: roughly 225 to 275 years, from the register's planting band of 1750 to 1800
trees.story:
The national register does not usually tell you a tree is going to die. About this one it does.

In the 1990s the ground it roots in was compacted, which for a beech is close to the worst thing that can be done to it: the fine feeding roots sit in the top half metre of soil and they need air in it. The tree took a blow it never came back from. The ground has since been improved and its condition has not recovered, and the register states plainly that it will in time have to be felled.

It is the oldest tree in Leeuwarden, banded 1750 to 1800, standing by a church whose history runs back to the fifteenth century and which has been reworked repeatedly for the different uses it has been put to.

There is nothing tragic to look at. A declining old beech is still an enormous dark thing on a city street, and the decline is mostly visible in what is missing: thinner cover at the top of the crown, more light coming through than there should be, dead ends on the upper branches.

This is the only tree on this site we would tell you to see sooner rather than later.
verified_sources: https://www.monumentalebomen.nl/
trees.access: Free. Stands on the street by the church, reachable at any time.
trees.transport: About 800 m north of Leeuwarden station, on foot.
trees.how_to_recognise: The large purple-leaved beech beside the Westerkerk on the Sint Anthonystraat, with a noticeably thin upper crown.

trees.name: The Beech at the Pier Pander Temple
trees.age_estimate: roughly 175 to 185 years, from the register's planting band of 1840 to 1850

location.address: Prinsentuin, at the Pier Pander temple

trees.story:
There is a small classical temple in this park, built in 1924 to hold the work of one sculptor.

Pier Pander was born in Friesland in 1864, the son of a rag merchant, and got out through talent and patronage: Rome, a career in marble, and an early death in 1919. The temple was raised to his own plans five years later, a domed round building in a public park, to house his sculpture. There are not many Dutch artists with a temple.

The beech stands beside it. Its date is not certain: the register bands it 1840 to 1850 and notes that trees here could equally have gone in when the temple was built, but photographs from the 1930s argue for the earlier reading. This is the Noorderplantage, laid out in 1843 on the former Noorderdwinger bastion and joined to the Prinsentuin at its eastern end, and the register's general conclusion is that the oldest trees in it date from between 1830 and 1880.

A beech beside a domed white building is a deliberate effect: smooth grey bark against smooth stone, and in summer a canopy dense enough to put the whole temple in shade.
verified_sources: https://www.monumentalebomen.nl/
trees.transport: About 1 km north of Leeuwarden station, on foot.
trees.how_to_recognise: The beech standing against the small domed temple at the western end of the park.

best_time.label: October to November: copper and russet, and young trees keep dead leaves all winter

trees.name: The Plane of the Old City Cemetery
trees.age_estimate: roughly 175 to 185 years, from the register's planting band of 1840 to 1850

location.address: Oude Stadsbegraafplaats, Jelsummerstraat, on the path between sections 2 and 3

trees.story:
Grey herons nest in the tops of these trees.

That is the first thing to know about the old city cemetery, and in February and March it is loud. Herons are colonial breeders, they choose tall trees near water, they start early in the year, and a heronry is not a quiet place: a large ragged nest per fork, birds arriving with sticks, and a noise like an argument in a shed. From below you mostly see the undersides and hear the rest.

The ground was laid out in 1833 to a design by Lucas Pieters Roodbaard, the same architect as the Prinsentuin, which is why a cemetery here reads like a landscape garden with graves in it. It went out of use long ago and is now a national monument. Ivy has taken many of the trunks.

The plane is on the path between sections two and three, banded 1840 to 1850, so from the earliest planting. London plane is the classic city tree because it sheds its bark in plates and with it the soot, which is why the trunk is a camouflage of cream, olive and grey.

Go in early spring, before the leaves, when you can see the birds.
verified_sources: https://www.monumentalebomen.nl/
trees.access: Free. Open ground, no longer in use as a cemetery.
trees.transport: About 1.5 km north of Leeuwarden station, on the Jelsummerstraat.
trees.how_to_recognise: Flaking cream and olive bark, on the path between sections 2 and 3. In late winter, the tree with heron nests in the top.

best_time.label: March, bare, with the heron colony visible in the crowns

trees.name: The Beech behind Tresoar
trees.age_estimate: roughly 155 to 165 years, from the register's planting band of 1860 to 1870
trees.story:
It stands next to the building where Friesland keeps its memory.

Tresoar is the Frisian historical and literary centre, the archive of a language with its own literature and its own long argument about being a language. The beech is directly behind it, in the Prinsentuin, on the line of the old northern fortifications that the park was built on and that have been a national monument since 1967.

The register bands it 1860 to 1870, which places it a generation after Roodbaard's layout rather than in it, planted into a park that already existed.

Beech is the tree that makes a Dutch park feel like a wood. It casts the heaviest shade of any large tree here, dense enough that almost nothing grows under a mature one, so the ground beneath is bare orange leaf litter and roots. That is not neglect, it is the tree winning.

Run your hand over the trunk. Beech bark stays smooth and thin its whole life, which is why people carve it, and why an old one in a public park usually carries a century of initials that have stretched and blurred as the trunk widened.
verified_sources: https://www.monumentalebomen.nl/
trees.transport: About 1 km north of Leeuwarden station, on foot.
trees.how_to_recognise: Smooth grey trunk, bare ground beneath, directly behind the library building.

best_time.label: October, when it turns copper and the litter goes orange

trees.name: The Ash by the Tea House
trees.age_estimate: roughly 145 to 155 years, from the register's planting band of 1870 to 1880

location.address: Prinsentuin, on the bank by the Theekoepel

trees.story:
The register calls this a very impressive specimen of the species and then adds, in the same breath, that its crown has developed one-sidedly because of the park trees standing next to it.

Both are true and the second explains the first. A tree that grows up hemmed in on one side puts everything it has into the open side, so you end up with an asymmetric crown reaching out over the path or the water, which reads as dramatic rather than damaged. Roodbaard's successors planted a park; the trees then negotiated among themselves.

It stands on the bank by the Theekoepel, the tea house, in the Noorderplantage end of the grounds, and the register bands it 1870 to 1880.

An ash of that age is worth stopping for now more than it was twenty years ago. Ash dieback, a fungal disease that arrived in the Netherlands in 2010, has killed a large share of the country's ash in the years since, and a tolerant mature tree is no longer an ordinary thing. A minority resist it, apparently on genetics rather than luck, and every big healthy one left is a candidate.

Black buds in winter, in opposite pairs. Nothing else here has them.
verified_sources: https://www.monumentalebomen.nl/
trees.transport: About 1 km north of Leeuwarden station, on foot.
trees.how_to_recognise: A big ash with a lopsided crown leaning away from its neighbours, on the slope by the tea house. Matt black buds in winter.

trees.name: The Marilandica Poplar
trees.age_estimate: roughly 145 to 155 years, from the register's planting band of 1870 to 1880

location.address: Prinsentuin, centrally, by the Noorder Stadsgracht

trees.story:
The trunk is the reason to come. It is deeply grooved and covered in burrs, hard woody swellings the size of fists and heads, which on a poplar of this age turn the bole into something closer to rock than bark.

Burrs are the tree's response to damage or infection: a knot of dormant buds that keeps growing without ever making a shoot, laying down wildly disordered grain. Woodturners prize the timber for exactly that and pay serious money for a burr this size. Standing on a public park bank by a city canal is the safest place it could be.

Marilandica is a named clone of the Canadian poplar, the hybrid of European black poplar and American cottonwood, selected and propagated by cuttings, which means every Marilandica anywhere is genetically the same tree. This one has been growing since the 1870s at the centre of the Prinsentuin by the Noorder Stadsgracht.

Poplars are planted for speed and taken out early because they get brittle. This one has been left, and a century and a half of being left is what produced the trunk.

Go and put your hands on it. That is the whole visit.
verified_sources: https://www.monumentalebomen.nl/
trees.transport: About 1 km north of Leeuwarden station, on foot.
trees.how_to_recognise: Centrally in the park by the canal, the tree with a deeply furrowed trunk covered in large woody burrs.

trees.name: The Feather Elms of Molenstraat

location.address: Molenstraat, opposite house numbers 29 and 35, Leeuwarden

trees.story:
The graft on this street elm has swollen into a collar of scar tissue with a circumference of more than five metres, wider at that single point than the trunk of almost anything else on this list.

Two feather elms, a narrow, upright cultivar of wych elm, stand about ten metres apart in an ordinary two by two metre planting pit on a residential street. Both were grafted roughly 1.5 metres above the ground when they were planted, a standard way to propagate this cultivar, and in the ninety-odd years since, the graft union on the larger of the two has ballooned far beyond the trunk it sits on.

An oak fern has taken root in the crown of that same tree, an epiphyte quietly living in the canopy of a street planting that most passersby probably read as unremarkable. The Dutch national register of monumental trees lists the pair under its dendrological category: official recognition for two elms that most of Molenstraat likely walks past without a second look.
verified_sources: Landelijk Register Monumentale Bomen (LRMB), entry nr 1682944, 'Pluimiepen Molenstraat'
https://bomenbieb.nl/bijzondere-bomen/pluimiep-leeuwarden/
trees.transport: About 1.2 km north of Leeuwarden station, on foot.
trees.how_to_recognise: Two tall, narrow elms opposite house numbers 29 and 35. The larger of the pair carries a huge swollen collar about 1.5 metres up the trunk, where it was grafted.

trees.name: The White Horse Chestnut of Poptaslot

location.neighbourhood: Front/side garden of Poptaslot, a 17th-century almshouse estate near Leeuwarden, about 4km from Leeuwarden's published lee_003

trees.story:
Left to itself, this horse chestnut would surround itself with children. Its lowest branches sweep down to the grass and will root wherever they rest, throwing up a ring of new stems around the parent trunk. The gardener at Poptaslot cuts them back so the tree stays one tree.

It was planted in 1840 by L.P. Roodbaard, the landscape architect who redrew country estate after country estate across Friesland in the loose English style, as part of his design for the grounds here. Three maples nearby are his too, the same year, the same job. Poptaslot, also called Heringastate, was already a seventeenth century almshouse estate when he arrived, so the chestnut has spent its whole life as the newest thing on old ground.

The trunk is 4.75 metres round and the tree is 19 metres tall. In June 2017 the national tree foundation put it first on its list of the ten most beautiful trees in Friesland, ahead of older and larger trees. Not the oldest, not the biggest, just the one people wanted to stand under.

The garden is free, on weekdays from April to September, roughly nine to four and later in high summer, closed on Sundays. Going inside the house is a guided tour and a separate arrangement, but the tree is in the garden and the garden is the free part.

best_time.label: May, when the white candles come out all over the crown

verified_sources: https://bomenbieb.nl/bijzondere-bomen/witte-paardenkastanje-poptaslot/
https://marssum.info/kastanjeboom-poptaslot-mooiste-van-friesland/
https://www.bomenstichting.nl/monumentalebomen/bomen-van-de-ereklasse/10-bijzondere-bomen-in-friesland.html

trees.transport: Village of Marssum, near Leeuwarden; reachable by local bus, roughly 10-15 minutes from Leeuwarden centre by car.

trees.name: The Wilhelminaboom

location.address: Raadhuisplein, in front of the old town hall, Leeuwarden

verified_sources: https://www.monumentalebomen.nl/ (Landelijk Register Monumentale Bomen, nr 1684252, 'Hollandse linde Wilhelminaboom', planted band 1890-1900)

https://historischcentrumleeuwarden.nl/images/Publiek/Stadswandelingen-PDF/brochure-wandelingmonumentaal-groen-2022.pdf (gemeente Leeuwarden / Historisch Centrum Leeuwarden, 'Wandelroute Monumentaal Groen', June 2022, stop 4)
trees.access: Free, on the public Raadhuisplein square in front of the old town hall (het Stadhuis); the tree stands inside an ornamental iron fence but the square itself is open at all times.
trees.transport: About 600m (roughly 8 minutes on foot) from Leeuwarden Centraal station; in the city centre.
trees.story:
Most commemorative trees get a plaque. This one got a fence carrying the state sword, the sceptre and the orb.

The lime went into the Raadhuisplein in 1898, the year Wilhelmina took the throne at eighteen, and the city set the architect Hendrik Kramer to work on the ironwork around its bed. Gates face each street that meets the square. Crowned letter W's and halberds stand along the rails, with orange twigs, blossom and apples worked into the metal between them. It is a great deal of blacksmithing for one lime, and it tells you precisely how a small provincial capital felt about its new queen.

A tinted postcard from around 1910 shows the result a decade in: a young tree inside a fence that already looks the more permanent of the two. The fence has not changed since. The tree has had a century and a quarter to catch up.

The date holds up from two directions. The city's own monumental-green walking route puts the planting at 1898, and the national register separately lists a Hollandse linde at this coordinate with a planting band of 1890 to 1900.

Fifty years later Leeuwarden planted a second royal lime a few hundred metres north, for Wilhelmina's daughter Juliana. Both are still standing.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the ornamental iron fence around its bed, worked with crowned W's, halberds and the state sword, sceptre and orb. It stands alone on the Raadhuisplein, in front of the old town hall.

best_time.label: late June and early July, when the lime flowers and the scent hangs over the square

trees.name: The Julianaboom

location.address: Jacobijnerkerkhof, near the entrance to the Boshuizen Gasthuis, Leeuwarden

verified_sources: https://www.monumentalebomen.nl/ (Landelijk Register Monumentale Bomen, nr 1683830, 'Hollandse linde Julianaboom', planted band 1940-1950)

https://historischcentrumleeuwarden.nl/images/Publiek/Stadswandelingen-PDF/brochure-wandelingmonumentaal-groen-2022.pdf (gemeente Leeuwarden / Historisch Centrum Leeuwarden, 'Wandelroute Monumentaal Groen', June 2022, stop 7 and top-10 entry IX)
trees.access: Free, in the public square around the Jacobijnerkerk (Grote Kerk); the tree stands in a rectangular bed in the north-west corner of the churchyard, open at all times.
trees.transport: About 850m (roughly 11 minutes on foot) from Leeuwarden Centraal station; in the city centre.
trees.story:
Leeuwarden's official list of its ten most special trees includes one that people now living watched go into the ground.

A photograph from 1948 shows alderman M.H. Geerts with a spade in front of the double gateway of the Boshuisen Gasthuis. The lime he is planting is still there, in the same rectangular bed in the north-west corner of the Jacobijnerkerkhof, and it carries the name of Princess Juliana. The country was three years out of the German occupation. The city planted a tree for the heir to the throne and had the alderman photographed doing it.

At 78 it is young for a register that mostly deals in centuries, and the national register does carry it: a Hollandse linde at this coordinate, planting band 1940 to 1950, which is about as close to a countersignature on the 1948 date as a register gets.

Behind it stands the gateway of the Boshuisen Gasthuis, an almshouse founded in 1652 by Anna van Eysinga, which makes the lime by nearly three centuries the newest thing on the corner. The Jacobijnerkerk takes up the rest of the square.

Two limes, two queens, fifty years and a few hundred metres apart, and both still standing.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the rectangular bed it stands in on its own, in the north-west corner of the churchyard around the Jacobijnerkerk. It stands in front of the double gateway of the Boshuisen Gasthuis.

best_time.label: late June and early July, when it flowers and the churchyard fills with the sound of bees

trees.name: The Horse Chestnut of Noorderweg

location.address: Noorderweg, beside the walking path near the Noorderbrug and the Stedelijk Gymnasium, Leeuwarden

verified_sources: https://www.monumentalebomen.nl/ (Landelijk Register Monumentale Bomen, nr 1682934, 'Witte paardenkastanje Noorderbrug', planted band 1900-1910)

https://historischcentrumleeuwarden.nl/images/Publiek/Stadswandelingen-PDF/brochure-wandelingmonumentaal-groen-2022.pdf (gemeente Leeuwarden / Historisch Centrum Leeuwarden, 'Wandelroute Monumentaal Groen', June 2022, top-10 entry III, dated 1899)
trees.access: Free, beside the public walking path along the Noorderweg/Arendstuin between the Noorderbrug and the Stedelijk Gymnasium.
trees.transport: About 1.1km (roughly 13 minutes on foot) from Leeuwarden Centraal station.
trees.story:
This chestnut made the city's top ten on the strength of one branch.

The monumental-green walking route that the gemeente publishes with the Historisch Centrum names ten trees as Leeuwarden's most special, and the entry for this one turns almost entirely on a single zware gesteltak: a heavy, low main limb that leaves the trunk and reaches out over the footpath. You meet it on the far side of the Stedelijk Gymnasium, on the stretch of the Noorderweg between the Noorderbrug and the flower shop Blomke fan Romke.

The two sources do not quite agree on when it went in. The brochure says 1899. The national register, which carries it as a witte paardenkastanje by the Noorderbrug, gives a planting band of 1900 to 1910. The disagreement is a year or so wide and settles nothing important: this is a tree from the turn of the twentieth century, so somewhere between 116 and 127 years old.

It has been putting that limb out over the path for longer than anyone now walking under it has been alive, through two wars, the arrival of the cars and every set of schoolchildren the gymnasium has sent past.

In May the crown goes up in white candles, the low limb included, which is the week to look at the branch that got it listed.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the one heavy limb that leaves the trunk low down and reaches out over the footpath, well below the rest of the crown. It stands on the Noorderweg between the Noorderbrug and the Stedelijk Gymnasium.

best_time.label: May, when the white candles stand up across the whole crown, low limb included

trees.name: The Oriental Plane of Stationsplein

location.address: Stationsplein, Leeuwarden (in front of the railway station)

verified_sources: https://www.monumentalebomen.nl/ (Landelijk Register Monumentale Bomen, nr 1682915, 'Oosterse plataan Stationsplein', planted band 1900-1910)

https://historischcentrumleeuwarden.nl/images/Publiek/Stadswandelingen-PDF/brochure-wandelingmonumentaal-groen-2022.pdf (gemeente Leeuwarden / Historisch Centrum Leeuwarden, 'Wandelroute Monumentaal Groen', June 2022, top-10 entry V, dated circa 1900)
trees.access: Free, on the public square directly in front of Leeuwarden railway station.
trees.transport: At Leeuwarden Centraal station, on the station square itself.
trees.story:
Step off the train at Leeuwarden and the first old tree you meet is the wrong plane.

Almost every plane on a Dutch square is a London plane, the hybrid bred for city air and planted by the thousand. This one is the parent species, an Oriental plane, which is rare this far north and which the national register carries under its Dutch name, oosterse plataan, at the Stationsplein.

It has held the open ground in front of the station since about 1900. Both sources that carry it agree: the city's own list of its ten most special trees dates it circa 1900, and the register gives a planting band of 1900 to 1910, so it is somewhere between 116 and 126 years old. The crown has spread the way planes on open squares do, low and wide over the paving, with the station front behind it.

Which means every arrival in this city by rail for more than a century has walked past it, most of them watching the clock rather than the tree. It stood there through the war and through the century of traffic that has crossed this square since.

Nobody has taped its girth. If you have a tape measure and a few minutes between trains, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the broad, low-spreading crown standing on its own out in the open paving. It stands on the Stationsplein directly in front of the railway station, with the station building behind it.

trees.name: The Variegated Maple of Rengerspark

location.address: Rengerspark, just inside the entrance on Spanjaardslaan, Leeuwarden

verified_sources: https://www.monumentalebomen.nl/ (Landelijk Register Monumentale Bomen, nr 1695808, 'Bontbladige esdoorn Rengerspark', planted band 1900-1910)

https://historischcentrumleeuwarden.nl/images/Publiek/Stadswandelingen-PDF/brochure-wandelingmonumentaal-groen-2022.pdf (gemeente Leeuwarden / Historisch Centrum Leeuwarden, 'Wandelroute Monumentaal Groen', June 2022, top-10 entry VI, dated 1904)
trees.access: Free, inside the public Rengerspark (a former private gift to the city, opened 1904, rijksmonument since 2001), just left of the entrance gate on Spanjaardslaan.
trees.transport: About 1.2km (roughly 15 minutes on foot) from Leeuwarden Centraal station.
trees.story:
The park gate carries 1904 in its ironwork, and so, near enough, does the tree standing just inside it.

Rengerspark was a private gift. In 1902 the former mayor W.J. van Welderen baron Rengers and his wife handed the ground to the city, Hendrik Copijn laid it out, and it opened in 1904 with more than fifty labelled tree species in it. A few steps inside the entrance on the Spanjaardslaan stands a sycamore of the cultivar 'Leopoldii', which the city's list of its ten most special trees names outright and dates to that opening year. The national register agrees within a decade: a bontbladige esdoorn on the south side of the park, planting band 1900 to 1910.

Spring is when the cultivar earns its place. The new leaves come out mottled pink, cream and green rather than plain green, as though somebody had been careless with the paint, and they hold that colouring for weeks before darkening. Nothing about it is accidental. Somebody choosing the trees for a brand new park in 1904 wanted a maple that would do this at the gate, and 122 years later it still does.

The park became a rijksmonument in 2001, which put Copijn's layout under protection. The maple has stood through the whole of it, and through the two wars that came in between.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the leaves, mottled pink, cream and green rather than plain green. It stands just inside the park's Spanjaardslaan entrance gate, the one whose ironwork carries the year 1904.

best_time.label: late April and May, when the new leaves open mottled pink and cream before they darken

trees.access: Free to view from Willemskade street; the tree stands in the garden of a private 19th-century villa (a national heritage building, built 1874) along the boundary facing the street. Register marks it visitable=ja and visible=ja.
trees.transport: About 1km south of Leeuwarden Centraal station, along the Willemskade waterfront.
trees.story:
For most of its life this beech was half of something else.

Two copper beeches went into the garden at Willemskade 27 around 1865, close enough together that over the decades they grew into and through one another. The IVN's walking guide to Leeuwarden's monumental trees calls them relatiebomen and still describes a pair. That guide has been overtaken. The national register's own history for the entry records that the southern tree was felled in 2026 after a fungus weakened its base, a problem first written up at an inspection in 2023. The northern beech is the one left standing, and it is the one on this page.

It was in the ground before the house was. The villa behind it, now a listed building, went up in 1874; the register gives the trees a planting band of 1860 to 1870 and the IVN says circa 1865, which puts this one at roughly 160 years old. The municipality designated it and entered it in the national register in 1988.

You look at it from the pavement. It stands along the garden boundary facing the Willemskade, on private ground with a public view, which is how the waterfront has seen it for a century and a half. In late April the new leaves open translucent red before they darken, and for a fortnight the whole crown holds the light.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its dark purple leaves, the single beech now left on the garden boundary at Willemskade 27, where a fused pair stood until 2026. It faces the street, in front of the 1874 villa.

best_time.label: late April and May, when the new leaves open translucent red before they darken
